title: KernelProbeArtifact
description: The `-Pout=` output of `./gradlew :adapter:kernelProbe`: what the REAL A12 kernel's runtime entry points reported, per request row and PER KERNEL STRATEGY — `validateFull` always, and `compute` when the request asked for it. Deterministic by construction — messages and computed outcomes are totally ordered, the header carries no clock reading, and the renderer pins a `\n` indenter — so two runs over identical input and an identical source tree produce identical bytes and a consumer can pin the artifact by SHA-256. The normative contract is docs/KERNEL-PROBE-SPEC.md.
$comment: `rows` stays required and is [] for a model-level-only request: it is a key of schemaVersion 1 that consumers already read, so making it optional would change the shape of artifacts they pin.

schemaVersion.description: this artifact shape's version; bumped when a key's presence or meaning changes. An artifact stays readable after the producer moves on because it carries its own version. The optional `computations` and `partialMessages` blocks did NOT bump it, for the same reason in both cases: a consumer receives such a block only by asking for it, so no artifact any existing consumer can obtain changes shape and no existing key changes meaning — while bumping would have broken the harder guarantee, that an unchanged request keeps producing byte-identical output that an already-pinned SHA-256 still matches. **The `fault` block did not bump it either, and it is the one addition that relaxed an existing REQUIRED key**: a block that raised omits `messages`. No artifact obtainable before `fault` existed can carry it — such a run produced no artifact at all — so no pinned bytes change and no key changes meaning; but a consumer holding the earlier v1 schema must tolerate a missing `messages` when `fault` is present, which is announced here rather than only in the producer's source.

producer.description: what produced the observation. A12-dmkits owns kernel invocation, engine identity, and this schema; the consumer owns pinning the bytes.

dmtoolVersion.description: the a12-dmkits release that ran the probe, or `(unknown)`

builtAgainst.description: the kernel version pin the probe compiled against

runtime.description: the kernel jar actually on the classpath, read from its own manifest. May be NEWER than `builtAgainst` — the project's F11 tolerance posture — so the two are reported separately rather than collapsed.

revision.description: the full 40-character Git revision of the producing tree, or `(unknown)`

state.description: whether the REVISION or the WORKTREE produced this observation: `CLEAN` means the tree matched `revision` exactly, `DIRTY` that tracked or untracked content differed from it, so the artifact is not reproducible from `revision` alone. Measured by the same program that stamps dmtool's own version resource.

request.description: the request's own inputs, echoed so the artifact states what it observed

model.description: the model reference, verbatim as the request spelled it

locale.description: the evaluation locale in A12's `language_COUNTRY` form; it decides the `message` channel's language and nothing else, and the kernel refuses a locale the model does not declare

clock.description: the pinned evaluation instant; ABSENT when the request pinned none, in which case the real clock was used and a clock-reading rule will not reproduce

mandatoryInformation.description: the kernel's mandatory-information derivation over the model's rule collection (`IRuleCollectionMetaInformation.getMandatoryInformationFromRules`) — a MODEL-level observation, so it appears once rather than per row or per strategy, and it reads no document. **It is the one observed channel whose raise still loses the run**: it is derived before the per-strategy engines exist, so there is no engine block to publish a `fault` on. Stated rather than captured — a model-level fault would need a top-level key of its own, and this project has no reproducer for a raise in this derivation. ABSENT unless the request asked for it, which is what keeps every already-pinned artifact byte-identical. The kernel derives these from rule CONDITIONS: `FieldNotFilled(/A/a)` makes `/A/a` mandatory, `GroupNotFilled(/A)` makes `/A` a mandatory root group, and a starred form makes neither because it does not hold for every repetition. Each list is sorted: the kernel returns `Set<String>`, which carries no order contract, so an artifact pinned by SHA-256 cannot depend on one. The rule collection is the kernel's own and unfiltered, so it includes the generated self-validation of every computation.

mandatory.description: `getMandatory()` — the fields the rule collection makes mandatory outright, sorted

mandatoryForRootGroup.description: `getMandatoryForRootGroup()` — the fields mandatory once their root group is present, sorted. A mandatory field is also mandatory regarding its root group.

mandatoryRootGroups.description: `getMandatoryRootGroups()` — the root groups the collection makes mandatory, sorted

dynamicEnumerations.description: the kernel's dynamic-enumeration derivation over the model's rule collection (`IRuleCollectionMetaInformation.getDynamicEnumerationStringValues`) — a MODEL-level observation, so it appears once rather than per row or per strategy, and it reads no document. ABSENT unless the request asked for it, which is what keeps every already-pinned artifact byte-identical. **This is the only route to the derivation the tool has**: its checker (`DynamicEnumerationService`) is constructed at two sites in the kernel — this facade method, and a facade factory with no in-kernel caller — and neither sits on a consistency rule, so its twelve `MVK_DYNENUM_*` / `MVK_ERROR_*` classes cannot be produced by `model check` or `rule check` however the model is shaped. **`diagnostics` is NOT a defect list.** The derivation checks EVERY rule and reports one problem for each that is not a dynamic enumeration IN FORM — measured: an ordinary single-leaf rule draws `MVK_DYNENUM_INVALID_GATE`, an ordinary conjunction `MVK_DYNENUM_INVALID_CALCOP` — so on a model of ordinary rules the block carries roughly one entry per rule and none of them is a fault. Read it as "which rules are dynamic enumerations, and why the rest are not".

valuesByField.description: each dynamic-enumeration field's full name mapped to the constant values the kernel extracted for it, keyed by field name so the order is deterministic under a SHA-256 pin

diagnostics.description: every problem the derivation reported, in the kernel's own order

code.description: the class the kernel named (e.g. `MVK_DYNENUM_INVALID_GATE`), or null when its message carried none

rule.description: the rule the kernel's own message attributed the problem to, or null when it named none — the usual case for this derivation, which is why a per-rule attributed verdict is `KernelAdapter.dynamicEnumerationDiagnostics(ruleFullName)` rather than this block

rows.description: one entry per request row, in request order; EMPTY when the request observed only model-level entry points, which read no document

enginesAgree.description: whether every strategy in `engines` produced the identical observation — EVERY channel its block reports — `messages`, `computations`, `partialMessages` and `fault` alike — not the messages alone. Two strategies that raised the SAME fault agree; one that raised beside one that did not disagrees. DERIVED from `engines`, never asserted independently — the per-strategy blocks are always both present, so a disagreement is visible in full rather than merged away. A strategy observed for compute never agrees with one that was not. `false` is a KERNEL FACT to record: the production-normative strategy is `kernel-groovy-dynamic` and a `kernel-java-static` split is characterized, never adopted (docs/CONFORMANCE-CORPUS-SPEC.md §11).

engines.description: one complete observation per kernel strategy

engine.description: the kernel codegen strategy that produced these messages, in the conformance corpus' vocabulary. `kernel-groovy-dynamic` is the production-normative anchor; `kernel-java-static` is the kernel's own validator generated as Java and compiled in memory.

messages.description: every message this strategy's `validateFull` raised, in a total order over the published channels. Ordering is by `code`, then `field`, `type`, `severity`, `referenced`, `fillToFix`, `message` — never kernel emission order, which nothing guarantees to be stable. Duplicates are retained, so a per-row rule firing on K rows appears K times.

fault.description: this strategy RAISED instead of observing this row, and the raise is published where the channels it prevented would have gone. PRESENT exactly when the kernel threw a RuntimeException, which is the class the measured reproducer belongs to (`FaultException`); an `Error` — an in-memory compilation failure, a `StackOverflowError` from a pathological model — is deliberately NOT caught and still ends the run with no artifact, because catching it would mean continuing on a JVM whose state we have not measured; a block that carries it carries NO channel key at all — `messages` absent rather than `[]`, because an empty message list beside a raise reads as `the kernel found no problem`, which is the misreading this artifact exists to prevent. The run keeps going: sibling rows and the other strategy are still observed, the artifact is still written and pinnable, and the process exits non-zero at the end. `enginesAgree` covers a fault like any other channel, so two strategies raising identically is a stated AGREEMENT rather than an unstated one.

observation.description: where the raise happened. The first three are the request's own `observe` names — the channel that threw, and the block ends there, because a strategy that cannot validate a document is not one whose compute answer means anything. `documentInstance` is a raise deserializing the row's document, before any channel could be read — **not observed on kernel 30.8.1**: two malformations (an object where a String field's value belongs, and the root group as a bare scalar) are both TOLERATED by the deserializer, which keeps unreadable content rather than refusing the document, so this locus is defensive rather than demonstrated (locked as a non-observation by `adapter.laws.KernelProbeFaultCaptureTest`). `engineBuild` is a raise building this strategy's engine, which is per REQUEST rather than per row, so it appears on every row of that strategy — that is the blast radius of one failed build, not a repeated measurement; it has no reproducer either, so the three CHANNEL loci are the observed ones.

chain.description: the cause chain, THROWN EXCEPTION FIRST, then each `getCause()` in turn (bounded at 16 links and cycle-safe). `type` is the exception's fully qualified class name and is stable across machines; `message` is whatever the kernel wrote and is deliberately NOT normalized — a message we rewrote would not be the observation. So if a particular raise embeds environment-specific detail (a temp path from the static-Java codegen, say), a fault-carrying artifact is byte-stable only as far as that text is; compare `type` when you need a machine-independent key.

type.description: the throwable's fully qualified class name

message.description: the throwable's message, ABSENT when it carried none — never rendered as an empty string

partialMessages.description: every message this strategy's `validatePart` raised under the row's declared `relevant` coverage, in the same total order as `messages`. PRESENT exactly when the request asked for `validatePart`; ABSENT otherwise. Unlike `messages`, an EMPTY array here is a measurement rather than a shape artifact: the `noneRelevant` coverage legitimately produces one, and that is one of the two things this observation exists to reach. Compare against `messages` on the same row to read what the caller's coverage gated: `validateFull` answers the document, `validatePart` answers the document AS SEEN BY a caller, and only the second can express a call-local partial coverage.

computations.description: what this strategy's `compute()` reported. PRESENT exactly when the request asked for it (`observe: ["validateFull", "compute"]`); ABSENT otherwise — absent means NOT OBSERVED, never `nothing computed`, which is why the block is omitted rather than rendered empty. `enginesAgree` covers it: a computation-only split between the strategies is as much a kernel fact as a message split.

outcomes.description: one entry per computed field instance the run reported, sorted by `field` and then by the remaining channels — never the order the kernel's result channels enumerate. A computed field the run did not report at all is absent from this list, which is distinct from being cleared.

field.description: the computed field instance's address (`IComputedFieldInstance.pointer`), in the SAME published form as a message `field` — canonical A12 when it names one cell, which a computed instance's address always does. Canonical A12 means no leading slash and `[1]` OMITTED, so the FIRST repetition of a repeatable level is written bare: `Basket/Lines/Total` is row 1 and `Basket/Lines[3]/Total` is row 3. That omission is A12's own form (`DocumentPointerImpl.toString`; an absent bracket means repetition 1), which is why this artifact does not emit `[1]` even though every per-row address would then carry an index. Two consequences for a consumer joining outcomes back to document rows. (1) A bare level is repetition 1, never 'no repetition' — count levels against the MODEL, not brackets in the string. (2) A form-level (non-repeating) outcome and row 1 of a repeatable group are therefore indistinguishable as strings — `Basket/Subtotal` and `Basket/Lines/Total` are both bracket-free — so which levels repeat is a model fact this address does not restate. The kernel's deprecated `getPath()` spelling is deliberately not published: one artifact, one address contract.

cleared.description: the kernel EMPTIED a target that was filled in the input without computing a new value for it (`getClearedFieldInstances`) — the precondition did not apply, or an operand was invalid. A cleared outcome carries NO `value` key; see `value`.

errored.description: the computed value was formally invalid for its target (`getComputedFieldInstancesWithErrors`). NOT the same as having no value: the kernel returns an out-of-range computed number and flags it, so an errored outcome may still carry `value`. An instance is never both `errored` and `cleared`.

value.description: the computed text (`IComputedFieldInstance.getStringValue`). ABSENT on a cleared outcome, present otherwise — which is how a cleared field is told apart from one that computed the empty string, a distinction this key's absence is the only carrier of. The absence is a DELIBERATE normalization, not a passthrough: measured 2026-08-12, a cleared instance's `getStringValue()` is `Optional.of("")` — present and empty for EVERY clear, and not an echo of the input cell it erased — so forwarding it would publish `""` for every clear and alias the two states. Locked by `adapter.laws.ComputeResultChannelsLawsTest`. Whether a genuine computed empty string is reachable is per result type and NOT settled here: `INTERPRETER-FINDINGS` IF123 measures the empty-store gate on the kernel's `VkString` arm only, and records that `VkBigDecimal` has no empty arm at all; custom field types and the date family are unmeasured. So this key's two-state contract is a guarantee of the SHAPE, held whether or not a given kernel reaches both states.

formalErrorsInOperands.description: the kernel's PRE-COMPUTATION formal validation of operand fields (`getFormalErrorsInOperands`). Per `IDocumentRtService.compute`: before any computation runs, every NON-COMPUTED field that is an operand of any computation is formally validated, and `Regardless of the formal errors found, computations will be performed. Any computations relying directly or indirectly on invalid fields will be skipped.` So this is an INVENTORY, not a causal attribution: it is emitted whether or not a computation was skipped, and it names no edge to the outcome it explains — a consumer that wants the link joins the two channels itself, using the kernel's skip guarantee. Two consequences it is easy to get wrong. (1) It is NOT a projection of `outcomes`: a field cleared by an unmet precondition appears in `outcomes` and contributes nothing here, and a formal error on a field that is an operand of nothing appears in `messages` and not here. (2) `non-computed` is the owner's word and is load-bearing: a field cleared because the computation it read was itself ERRORED names nothing here, because a computed field is out of this channel's scope by definition (see `getComputedFieldInstancesWithErrors` + its `getErrorMessage`, which the probe does not publish). The exact operand set — including every field CONTAINED by a referenced group, which no runtime read need touch — is the kernel's `CalculationOperandsCollector`, locked by `adapter.laws.ComputationEagerPrepassLawsTest`. Same records and same ordering as `messages`, so one parser reads both — including the address form, so a formal error on an operand in the FIRST repetition is written bare (`Basket/Lines/Surcharge`) exactly as an outcome is; see `outcomes[].field`.

message.description: one kernel `IMessage`, carrying the key names of a `model eval` `messages[]` entry so one parser reads dmtool's runtime output and this artifact alike. Used for both the validation channel and the compute run's operand formal errors.

code.description: the rule's error code, or a kernel formal-check code

field.description: the offending field's address (`IMessage.getErrorFieldPointer`). Canonical A12 pointer — no leading slash, `[1]` omitted — exactly when the address names ONE cell; otherwise, when it carries a wildcard or a level that matched no row, the interpreter house form (`/Order[1]/Items[0]/Quantity`), because A12 defines no pointer string for such a value. Test the leading slash to tell them apart.

type.description: A12's value-vs-omission typing (`IMessage.getMessageType`): OMISSION_ERROR means filling more fields could clear it, VALUE_ERROR that what is entered is wrong

message.description: the kernel's fully interpolated end-user text (`IMessage.getErrorText`) at the request's locale, with every `$Field$` token resolved against this document

referenced.description: the fields the rule READ — its operands (`IMessage.getReferencedFieldsPointers`), sorted. Same per-address form contract as `field`, decided per address: one message legitimately shows both spellings. Sorted rather than in kernel emission order, which nothing guarantees to be stable and which an artifact pinned by SHA-256 cannot depend on; no position is being discarded, since this channel is compared as a set everywhere it is compared.

fillToFix.description: for an OMISSION_ERROR, the operand fields whose filling could clear it (`IMessage.getRefOmissionErrorResponsiblePointers`) — measured to be ALL of the rule's operands, not only the empty ones; EMPTY for a VALUE_ERROR. Same per-address form contract as `field`, and sorted for the same reason as `referenced`.
